title: Systematic construction of multiqubit unextendible product bases
abstract: The construction of multiqubit unextendible product bases (UPBs) has been a long-standing problem. We give a systematic construction of multiqubit UPBs by studying their unextendible orthogonal matrices (UOMs) with graph-theoretic methods. Row decompositions of small UOMs produce the main intervals. Com- pletion graphs settle the remaining small UPB sizes, except for one size obtained from a good column structure. Nonexistence of the other UPB sizes follows from counts of fibres and row pairs. The computer is used only for a few finite UOM checks, whose exact tests are stated in the certificate appendix. These arguments determine the complete multiqubit UPB size spectrum in every dimension.
summary: This paper provides a comprehensive, systematic mathematical construction for multiqubit unextendible product bases (UPBs). By translating the problem into the study of unextendible orthogonal matrices (UOMs) and applying graph theory, the authors determine the exact size spectrum for these crucial quantum structures. This work advances the theoretical understanding of resource constraints in multiqubit quantum information processing.
main_problem: The paper systematically determines the complete size spectrum for multiqubit unextendible product bases (UPBs).
main_result: The authors provide a complete characterization of the possible sizes of multiqubit UPBs in every dimension, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for their existence.
method: The research employs advanced graph-theoretic methods, including analyzing unextendible orthogonal matrices (UOMs) via row decompositions and completion graphs.
model_or_system: The context is quantum information processing involving multiqubit systems. UPBs are mathematically linked to the structure of UOMs, which are orthogonal matrices representing product vectors.
key_observables: The primary observable is the set $\Theta_n$, representing the possible sizes $m$ for an $n$-qubit UPB.
important_parameters: The dimension $n$ (number of qubits) and the size $m$ (number of product vectors) are the key parameters. Specific constraints involve parity of $n$ and structural counts.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the formal matrix structure capturing the necessary information for the physical UPB realization, and the use of graph-theoretic theorems.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate various constructions (e.g., row-decomposition, matching core) of UOMs, demonstrating specific examples like $M_{13,9}$ and $M_{15,10}$ as valid structures.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the formal mathematical framework (UOMs, fibre supports), establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for extendibility (Theorem 4), and then applying graph theory to systematically determine the complete size spectrum $\Theta_n$ for all dimensions.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical characterization of UPBs provides fundamental constraints on quantum state properties, which is crucial for understanding entanglement measures and nonlocality in quantum information protocols.

Hence every new entry is the mate of the original entry given by the two subscripts. In (c)–(d), every black point represents a completion row. A line joins two orthogonal rows. The set C is marked by the dashed box.

Figure 4: The construction with two added columns. The two input UOMs use different alphabets. In each added column, the entries are constant on every decomposition block. The bars indicate the mate relation between the entries. The two factor graphs used for the added columns are shown in panels (b) and (c).

Figure 5: The lift of a square kernel. In panel (a), the one-factor M1 is added to the original factor F1. In panel (b), the permutation on A is kept, while every element of B is fixed. The full matrix obtained from the construction is given in panel (c), and panel (d) explains where each family of its entries comes from.

Figure 6: The joining of two lifted input UOMs by merging factor columns. All entries of the resulting matrix are given in panel (a). Panel (b) compares a pair of factor columns with the merged column. The same operation on the decomposition blocks is shown in panels (c)–(e). The four edges in panel (e) form the graph K2,2.

Figure 7: Odd padding used in Corollary 27. The 8 × 5 block is the original matrix Y5. The δ-entries give the five removed factors Dj on the new single rows. The π-entries give the factors Pℓ.
